title: WHAT HAPPENED IF A MAN HAD SEX WITH A WOMAN DURING HER MENSTRUAL PERIOD?
paragraphs: WHAT HAPPENED IF A MAN HAD SEX WITH A WOMAN DURING HER MENSTRUAL PERIOD?

Leviticus gives an answer severe enough to disturb modern readers—but if you stop at the punishment, you may completely miss what the blood, the boundary, and ultimately Jesus Christ were pointing toward.
There are verses in the Bible people quietly skip.
Not because they are difficult to read.
Because they are difficult to explain.
Leviticus 18:19 and Leviticus 20:18 belong to that category.
Maybe you have read them and wondered, Why would God care about this?
Maybe someone used these passages to argue that the Bible treats a woman’s menstrual cycle as shameful.
Maybe you have personally done what these verses prohibit, and now the question is no longer academic.
Did I commit some unforgivable sin?
Is menstruation somehow dirty before God?
Does this command still apply to Christians today?
And what exactly happened under the Law of Moses if a man knowingly had sexual intercourse with a woman during her menstrual period?
Those questions deserve something better than embarrassment, mockery, fear, or a convenient answer designed to make Scripture say whatever we want.
So stay with the text.
Because there is blood in this story.
There is holiness in this story.
There is judgment in this story.
But before we reach the end, there will be another kind of blood.
Blood that does not make the sinner unclean.
Blood that cleanses the unclean.
And that changes everything.
Leviticus 18:19 reads:
“You shall not approach a woman to uncover her nakedness while she is in her menstrual uncleanness.”
The Hebrew is striking:
וְאֶל־אִשָּׁה בְּנִדַּת טֻמְאָתָהּ לֹא תִקְרַב לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ
Ve’el-ishshah beniddat tum’atah lo tiqrav legalot ervatah.
In straightforward sense:
You shall not approach a woman during the menstrual state of her uncleanness to uncover her nakedness.
One important word is נִדָּה — niddah.
In this context it refers to the menstrual condition or period of separation associated with ritual impurity.
And immediately we need to destroy a damaging misunderstanding.
The Bible does not say that a woman sins simply by menstruating.
Read Leviticus 15 carefully.

Menstruation is treated within Israel’s system of ritual purity. Bodily discharges could produce a state of ceremonial uncleanness, and ceremonial uncleanness was not automatically the same thing as committing a moral transgression.
That distinction matters enormously.
A menstruating Israelite woman was not being accused of rebellion against God merely because her body was functioning naturally.
Her menstrual flow placed her in a condition described by the Hebrew vocabulary of ritual impurity.
That is different from saying:
She is disgusting.
Different from saying:
Her womanhood is sinful.
Different from saying:
God is ashamed of her body.
Scripture says none of those things.

In fact, the woman herself was not the only person who could become ritually unclean in Leviticus. Men experienced bodily discharges. People became unclean through contact with corpses. Childbirth involved purification regulations. Various physical conditions intersected with Israel’s elaborate system of clean and unclean.
God was teaching Israel to live with an extraordinary consciousness of distinction.
Holy and common.
Clean and unclean.
Life and death.
Approach and separation.
And blood occupied an especially important place in that world.
Leviticus 17:11 declares that the life of the flesh is in the blood.
So when we arrive at Leviticus 18:19, we are not reading an isolated sentence dropped randomly into the Bible.
We are standing inside Israel’s covenant world.
Then comes the verse that makes people uncomfortable.
Leviticus 20:18.
The Hebrew begins:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִשְׁכַּב אֶת־אִשָּׁה דָּוָה
Ve’ish asher-yishkav et-ishshah davah...
It describes a man lying sexually with a menstruating woman.
The text says that he has exposed her flow and she has uncovered the flow of her blood, and then comes the consequence:
וְנִכְרְתוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם מִקֶּרֶב עַמָּם
Venikhretu sheneihem miqqerev ammam.
“Both of them shall be cut off from among their people.”
There is the uncomfortable answer.

Under the Mosaic covenant, Leviticus 18:19 prohibited sexual intercourse during menstruation, and Leviticus 20:18 attaches the serious covenant sanction of being “cut off” from the people to the prohibited act.
Notice something else.
The text does not place responsibility only upon the woman.
It says:
שְׁנֵיהֶם — sheneihem.
“Both of them.”
The man cannot point at the woman and say, “She was the unclean one.”
Both are addressed.
Both crossed the stated boundary.
Both are accountable.
But then somebody who has actually read Leviticus may raise an important objection.
“What about Leviticus 15:24?”
Good question.
That passage says that if a man lies with a menstruating woman and her menstrual impurity comes upon him, he becomes unclean for seven days, and the bed on which he lies becomes unclean.
So why does one passage speak about seven days of uncleanness while another speaks about being cut off?

Interpreters have wrestled with the relationship between these texts. One common distinction understands Leviticus 15 within regulations governing ritual impurity and Leviticus 18 and 20 as addressing the prohibited sexual act itself within the holiness laws.
Whatever interpretive details are debated, we should not erase either passage.
Leviticus 15 describes ritual consequences associated with menstrual impurity.
Leviticus 18 explicitly says not to approach for sexual relations during that condition.
Leviticus 20 assigns a severe covenant consequence to violating that prohibition.
We have to let all three texts speak.
But now comes the question Christians cannot avoid:
Does that mean Christians today are living under the exact civil and ceremonial sanctions of ancient Israel?
No.
And understanding why does not require throwing Leviticus away.
Jesus did not come because the Old Testament was an embarrassing mistake that needed to disappear.
He came as its fulfillment.

The Law was part of God’s covenant dealings with Israel, containing moral instruction alongside sacrificial, priestly, purity, dietary, national, and ceremonial regulations that shaped Israel as a people set apart for God.
The New Testament does not simply transfer Israel’s entire ritual-purity system and its national covenant penalties unchanged onto the Church.
That is why Christians do not become ceremonially unclean for seven days because they touched something that Leviticus declared unclean.
That is why the Church does not maintain the Levitical sacrificial system.
That is why Christians do not bring animals to a Levitical priest after bodily discharges.
And most importantly, the New Testament never teaches that the ordinary biological process of menstruation makes a Christian woman spiritually condemned before God.
So we must be careful here.
A Christian should not take Leviticus 20:18 and announce that Christians who have intercourse during menstruation must now be expelled from society under ancient Israel’s covenant sanction.
That would ignore the covenantal setting of the command and the New Testament’s teaching concerning Christ and the Law.
At the same time, we should not become so desperate to escape an uncomfortable verse that we refuse to learn anything from it.
Because underneath this difficult passage stands a truth modern culture desperately resists:
God has authority even over the parts of our lives we call private.
Including sexuality.
That is where this ancient verse suddenly stops feeling ancient.
We live in a world that repeatedly whispers:
My body.
My desire.
My bedroom.
My rules.
But Scripture keeps confronting humanity with another reality.
You belong to your Creator.
And for the Christian, Paul makes the claim even more personal:
“You are not your own.”
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
—1 Corinthians 6:19–20
That principle reaches much further than one question about menstruation.
Because the deeper question is not merely:
What am I technically allowed to do?
The deeper question is:
Does Jesus have authority here too?
In my bedroom?
In my browser history?
In my secret fantasies?
In the relationship nobody knows about?
In what I do with another person’s body?
In what I do with my own?
In the desires I excuse because nobody sees them?
That is where Leviticus stops being a strange ancient book and starts becoming a mirror.
We love a Jesus who enters the visible parts of our lives.
Our Sunday mornings.
Our worship playlists.
Our inspirational posts.
Our Bible verses.
Our public testimonies.
But Jesus does not stand outside the locked rooms of human existence.
He is Lord there too.
And maybe that is why this subject makes us uncomfortable.
Sometimes the verses we most want to avoid are standing closest to the doors we most want to keep locked.
But hear this carefully.
Conviction is not the same thing as hopelessness.
If you crossed sexual boundaries in your past...
If you crossed them last night...
If your sexual history contains things you are ashamed even to name...
If you have lived for years believing that God could forgive everybody except you...
Do not turn an Old Testament purity passage into a declaration that Christ cannot cleanse you.
Because the Gospel moves us toward another scene involving blood.
A hill.
A cross.
A wounded Savior.
And suddenly the imagery becomes almost unbearable.
Throughout Scripture, blood is associated with life.
Sacrificial blood stood at the center of Israel’s worship.
And then Jesus Christ came.
Not as another sinner searching for cleansing.
But as the spotless Lamb.
At the Last Supper He spoke of His blood of the covenant.
At Calvary, He gave Himself.
Hebrews tells us that the sacrificial system found its decisive fulfillment in Christ, whose sacrifice does what repeated animal sacrifices could never finally accomplish.
And 1 John 1:7 gives sinners one of the most beautiful sentences ever written:
“The blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin.”
Do you see the reversal?
Human beings spend their lives trying to hide their uncleanness.
Jesus walks toward unclean people.
Human beings say, “Do not touch me. If you knew what I had done, you would leave.”
Jesus touches lepers.
Receives sinners.
Restores failures.
Calls the ashamed out of hiding.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because His grace is greater than the sinner’s ability to save himself.
The Gospel is not:
Your sin was never serious.
The Gospel is:
Your sin was so serious that Christ went to the cross—and His grace is so powerful that the cross is enough.
That distinction can change a life.
Maybe you came to this article because you wanted an answer about sex during menstruation.
You got the answer.

Ancient Israel was expressly forbidden from that sexual act in Leviticus 18:19, and Leviticus 20:18 describes both participants being “cut off” from their people for violating the prohibition. Leviticus 15 also provides the broader ritual-purity background.
But perhaps God allowed an uncomfortable question to bring you somewhere deeper.
Because maybe your real problem was never Leviticus.
Maybe your real question was:
Can Jesus still want me after everything I have done?
Yes.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus receives sinners and transforms sinners.
Biblical repentance is not learning better vocabulary for excusing what God calls sin.
It is turning toward God.
Confessing.
Surrendering.
Trusting Christ.
Walking differently because the One who forgave you is now the One you love.
And if something in this article exposed an area you have been hiding, do not perform spirituality for the comments.
Be honest before God.

And if Jesus has already brought you out of a place you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what Christ has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another ashamed person needs to read tonight.
Not everybody who needs this will search for it.
Sometimes they need a friend courageous enough to put it where they can find it.
Supporting Gospel work can be a genuine way of using what God has entrusted to us for ministry, teaching, discipleship, and the spread of biblical truth.
Paul wrote:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός.
Hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia... hilaron gar dotēn agapa ho Theos.
In essence: each should give as he has determined in his heart, not under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
—2 Corinthians 9:7
That is how Christian support should work.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Joyfully.
For God’s glory.
And there is something else we want people to know.
Share.
Pray.

Put biblical truth in front of the struggling believer who is quietly slipping away, the Christian trapped in shame, the seeker afraid to ask difficult questions, the lukewarm believer who needs awakening, or even the unbelieving friend who has never understood what Christianity is actually about.
Because the purpose was never merely to win an argument about Leviticus.
The purpose is to lead people through Scripture to Jesus.
And perhaps that is the truth worth carrying away from this uncomfortable passage:
God is holy.
Sin matters.
Our bodies matter.
Sexuality matters.
Obedience matters.
But your worst chapter does not possess greater authority than the cross of Jesus Christ.
You may have crossed boundaries.
You may have ignored God.
You may carry memories you wish you could erase.
You may feel unclean in places nobody else can see.
But if you come to Christ in repentance and faith, your scandal does not get the final sentence.

The blood that makes us ashamed of our humanity is not the blood that defines our eternity; for the repentant sinner, the final word belongs to the blood of Jesus Christ that cleanses, redeems, and brings us home.
